column1: negative — out-of-scope question about hillshade/terrain layers,skills/maplibre-fonts-glyphs/SKILL.md,How do I add a hillshade layer from a raster-dem source to my MapLibre GL JS style?,"Below is a complete, step-by-step recipe for adding a **hillshade** layer that is driven by a **raster-DEM** source to a MapLibre GL JS map.
Everything is shown in plain JavaScript (no build tools required) and can be dropped into a simple HTML page.

column3: Why it matters
Supplies elevation values (in meters) that the hillshade renderer turns into light/shadow.
The visual layer that draws the shaded relief.
Hillshade support was added in v2.0 (and works in all later versions).
The browser must be allowed to fetch the DEM tiles.
Hillshade is usually drawn on top of a plain background or a raster basemap.

column1: You can use any raster-DEM that follows the **Mapbox Terrain-RGB** encoding (or the newer **MapLibre Terrain-RGB**).

column3: URL template
column4: Notes

column3: `https://api.maptiler.com/tiles/terrain-rgb/{z}/{x}/{y}.png?key=YOUR_KEY`
column4: Free tier (up to 100 k tiles/month).

column3: `https://{s}.tile.opentopomap.org/terrain/{z}/{x}/{y}.png`
column4: No API key, but limited coverage.

column3: `https://myserver.com/dem/{z}/{x}/{y}.png`
column4: Full control, must pre-process to Terrain-RGB.

column1: > **Tip:** If you already have a GeoTIFF DEM, you can convert it to Terrain-RGB tiles with tools like **gdal2tiles.py** (`-t_srs EPSG:3857 -a_srs EPSG:4326 -r bilinear -z 0-14 -w none`).
// replace with your own URL template
// important: tell MapLibre that the tiles contain elevation data
// (the default is false for raster sources)
// The `encoding` property is optional; MapLibre assumes Terrain-RGB.
// encoding: ""mapbox""   // <-- uncomment if you use Mapbox Terrain-RGB
// a light basemap so you can see the hillshade contrast
// 4️⃣ Hillshade layer – the star of the show
// Optional visual tweaks (see docs for all options)
pitch: 45,          // tilt the map so the shading is visible
antialias: true    // improves hillshade quality on some browsers

column3: Code snippet
column4: Explanation

column3: `new maplibregl.Map({ … })`
column4: Creates the map container, sets a basic style object, and enables a 3-D view (`pitch`).

column3: `""terrain"": { type: ""raster-dem"", tiles: [...] }`
column4: Declares a **raster-DEM** source. The `type` is crucial – `raster` would *not* provide elevation data.

column3: `""osm-basemap""`
column4: A simple raster basemap so you can see the hillshade contrast. Not required; you could use a vector basemap instead.

column3: `""hillshade""`
column4: The actual hillshade renderer. It automatically reads the elevation values from the `terrain` source.

column3: `hillshade-illumination-direction`, `hillshade-exaggeration`, …
column4: Fine-tune lighting direction, shadow intensity, and exaggeration. All are optional; defaults work fine.

column3: Improves the visual quality of the hillshade on browsers that support WebGL antialiasing.
What to check / fix

The DEM tiles must be served with CORS headers that allow your page’s origin (or `*`). If you host the tiles yourself, add `Header set Access-Control-Allow-Origin ""*""` (Apache) or `add_header 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' '*';` (NGINX).
Hillshade only works with **Terrain-RGB** (or Mapbox-compatible) encoding. If you serve plain grayscale DEM tiles, they will be interpreted as colors and the shading will look wrong.
Accidentally using `""type"": ""raster""` will give you a normal raster image, not elevation data, and the hillshade layer will appear blank.
DEM tiles are usually available only up to a certain zoom (e.g., 14). If you zoom beyond that, the hillshade will stop rendering because no DEM tiles exist.
Hillshade is GPU-intensive. Keep `tileSize` at 256 (default) and avoid extremely high `hillshade-exaggeration` values, which can cause banding.

You can keep your vector style (roads, labels, etc.) and just add the hillshade layer on top of the raster basemap. Order matters: place the hillshade **after** the basemap but **before** any label layers you want to stay on top.

Some older mobile browsers lack WebGL2, which is required for the hillshade shader. Test on target devices; if you need a fallback, hide the hillshade layer (`map.setLayoutProperty('hillshade', 'visibility', 'none')`).

You can update the illumination direction on the fly:
`map.setPaintProperty('hillshade', 'hillshade-illumination-direction', 45);`

column1: Hillshade is usually drawn **under** most other layers (roads, labels, etc.) but **over** the base raster or vector background. If you need to adjust the order, use `map.moveLayer` or the `before` argument when adding the layer:
// Place hillshade just above the background but below everything else
map.addLayer(hillshadeLayer, 'waterway-label'); // insert before the first label layer

Open the file in a browser (or serve it via a local web server) and you should see a shaded relief map over the OpenStreetMap basemap.

column4: Fix

column3: DEM source not loading (404, CORS, wrong URL)
column4: Open the Network tab, verify tile requests succeed, and that the server sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin:*` (or your domain).

column3: DEM tiles contain **no data** (e.g., all zeros) or the wrong encoding
column4: Check the DEM values with a GIS viewer. If you’re using Mapbox’s `terrain-rgb` encoding, keep `encoding: ""mapbox""` (default).

column3: Using a low-resolution DEM (e.g., 256-px tiles at high zoom)
column4: Provide higher-resolution DEM tiles or increase `maxzoom` on the source.

column2: **Shadows move when you rotate the map**
column3: `hillshade-illumination-anchor` is set to `""map""` (default)
column4: Change to `""viewport""` if you want a fixed sun direction.

column3: The layer was added before the new style finished loading
column4: Always add sources/layers inside a `map.on('style.load', …)` handler, or re-add after `map.setStyle`.

column3: Server missing `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header
column4: Add the header on the server, or proxy the tiles through a CORS-enabled endpoint.

column3: How to achieve it
Call `map.setTerrain({ source: 'my-dem', exaggeration: 1.5 })` **after** adding the DEM source. Hillshade will still render as a 2-D overlay, giving a nice “relief-plus-terrain” effect.
Use a **style expression** for any paint property, e.g. `'hillshade-exaggeration': ['interpolate', ['linear'], ['zoom'], 5, 0.3, 12, 0.8]`.
Add each as a separate source and create separate hillshade layers, ordering the higher-resolution layer on top.

Bundle the DEM tiles (or a single COG) with your app and serve them from a local `file://` or `http://localhost` server. The same `raster-dem` source definition works; just point `url`/`tiles` to the local path.
